sentence: We will show that under the stated conditions the “friend‐graph” must have girth 5 – that is, the shortest cycle in the graph has 5 vertices.
sentence-category-reason: States the goal of the solution to be shown (girth 5), announcing the intended outcome.

sentence: Consequently, if we try to seat a group of residents around a table so that each person is next to a friend, the fewest number of people that can “close the cycle” is 5.
sentence-category-reason: Directly states the resulting minimal table size as 5, giving the problem's answer.

sentence: Below is one way to arrive at this conclusion.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces that a method will follow to reach the conclusion, outlining the approach.
Section separator indicating a transition with no mathematical content.

sentence: The Conditions and an Equation
sentence-category-reason: Section heading signaling a transition, not substantive problem-solving content.

sentence: Label the residents 1,…,n.
sentence-category-reason: Sets notation by labeling residents 1 to n, an operational setup step.

sentence: Declare two residents “friends” when the corresponding vertices are connected by an edge.
sentence-category-reason: Defines the graph model by declaring edges represent friendships, setting up notation.

sentence: The hypotheses are: (a) Every two residents who are not friends have at least one friend in common.
sentence-category-reason: Restates a given hypothesis from the problem about non-friends having a common friend.

sentence: (b) No one is a friend of everyone else.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the given hypothesis that no one is a friend of everyone.

sentence:
(c) If a₁,…,aₙ are the numbers of friends (“degrees”) of the residents then
  a₁² + a₂² + ⋯ + aₙ² = n² – n.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the given degree-squared sum condition from the problem.
Section separator indicating a transition with no substantive content.

sentence: The Degree‐Squared Sum Forces Regularity
sentence-category-reason: Section heading indicating the topic of the next argument.

sentence:
A standard application of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
  a₁² + ⋯ + aₙ² ≥ (1/n)(a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ)².
sentence-category-reason: Invokes Cauchy–Schwarz to derive a general inequality, explaining a relevant principle.

sentence: But the given sum is n² – n.
sentence-category-reason: Recalls the given numeric value of the sum from the problem statement.

sentence: (Also, by the handshake lemma a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ = 2e, where e is the number of edges.
sentence-category-reason: Cites the handshake lemma to relate the sum of degrees to edges, a theoretical relation.

sentence: ) A routine check shows that the equality case of Cauchy–Schwarz must hold here.
sentence-category-reason: Infers that equality holds in Cauchy–Schwarz, a logical deduction.

sentence: (In brief, if equality holds then all numbers a₁,…,aₙ are equal.
sentence-category-reason: Explains the equality condition of Cauchy–Schwarz implying equal degrees.

sentence: ) Thus every resident has the same number r of friends.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes regularity (same number r of friends) from the equality condition.

sentence:
Moreover, from a simple counting argument one deduces
  n·r² = a₁² + … + aₙ² = n² – n,
so  r² = n – 1  or  n = r² + 1.
sentence-category-reason: Carries out concrete algebraic deductions to obtain r² = n − 1 and n = r² + 1.

sentence: Thus the graph is regular of degree r and its number of vertices satisfies n = r² + 1.
sentence-category-reason: Summarizes the computed consequences: regular of degree r and n = r² + 1, following the calculation.

sentence: (It is easy to check that r can’t be n–1 because no one is allowed to be friends with everybody.
sentence-category-reason: Deduction from the condition that no one is friends with everyone; rules out r = n−1.
Section divider indicating a transition without mathematical content.

sentence: The “Unique Common Friend” Property
sentence-category-reason: Section heading announcing the next focus of the argument.

sentence: Now take any two residents who are not friends.
sentence-category-reason: Sets up the next step by selecting two non-friends to analyze.

sentence: By hypothesis (a) they have at least one common friend.
sentence-category-reason: Applies a given hypothesis to infer existence of a common friend.

sentence: In fact, one may count the number of pairs of non‐friends in two different ways (using the given sum of squares) to show that in fact every two non‐adjacent vertices must have exactly one common neighbor.
sentence-category-reason: Explains a double-counting argument to conclude uniqueness of common neighbor.

sentence:
In other words, the graph not only is regular but also has the property that
  if x and y are distinct and not adjacent, then |N(x) ∩ N(y)| = 1.
sentence-category-reason: Restates and formalizes the derived unique common neighbor property.

sentence: (Here N(x) denotes the set of neighbors of x.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces notation for neighbors, setting basic definitions.
Section divider indicating a transition.

sentence: No Triangles (and No 4‐cycles Either)
sentence-category-reason: Section heading announcing the next goal (excluding small cycles).

sentence: A basic observation now is that if x and y are friends then they cannot have a common neighbor.
sentence-category-reason: States a key inferred property about adjacent vertices sharing no common neighbor.

sentence: (Were there a vertex z adjacent both to x and y, then x and y would have two common neighbors – z would be one, and the unique common friend required for non‐adjacent pairs would force x and y to be non‐adjacent.
sentence-category-reason: Provides the reasoning showing why shared neighbors would contradict uniqueness.

sentence: ) Thus any two adjacent vertices have no common friend and in particular there are no 3–cycles (triangles) in the graph.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes from the reasoning that triangles do not exist.

sentence: Next, suppose for contradiction that some 4–cycle exists with vertices x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ and edges x₁x₂, x₂x₃, x₃x₄, x₄x₁.
sentence-category-reason: Initiates a proof by contradiction by assuming a 4-cycle exists.

sentence: Notice that x₁ and x₃ are not adjacent (otherwise x₁, x₂, x₃ would form a triangle).
sentence-category-reason: Infers non-adjacency of opposite vertices in a 4-cycle to avoid a triangle.

sentence: But then by the unique common–friend property, x₁ and x₃ should have exactly one common neighbor.
sentence-category-reason: Applies the unique common neighbor property to those non-adjacent vertices.

sentence: However, both x₂ and x₄ are common neighbors of x₁ and x₃.
sentence-category-reason: Observes that two vertices in the 4-cycle would both be common neighbors, contradicting uniqueness.

sentence: This contradiction rules out 4–cycles.
sentence-category-reason: Draws the conclusion from the contradiction that 4-cycles cannot exist.
Section divider indicating a transition.

sentence: Girth and Seating at a Round Table
sentence-category-reason: Section heading introducing the connection to girth and seating.

sentence: Since neither 3–cycles (triangles) nor 4–cycles exist, the shortest cycle in the graph (its girth) has length at least 5.
sentence-category-reason: Deducts girth ≥ 5 from absence of 3- and 4-cycles.

sentence: In fact, one may show (and indeed it is known for the only possible examples in this setting) that the girth is exactly 5.
sentence-category-reason: States a known fact refining the bound to girth exactly 5.

sentence: Now, “seating a set of residents at a round table in such a way that any two neighbors are friends” means we are choosing a cycle (not necessarily induced) of the friendship–graph.
sentence-category-reason: Interprets the problem setup by mapping seating to cycles in the graph.

sentence: The problem asks for the smallest number k (with k ≥ 3) such that such a seating is possible.
sentence-category-reason: Restates what the problem is asking for.

sentence: But since there is no cycle of length 3 or 4, the least number of people you may seat in a round table friendship–cycle is 5.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes the minimal seating size directly as 5 from the girth argument.
Section divider with no problem-solving content.

sentence: Summary of Possibilities
sentence-category-reason: Section heading indicating a transition.

sentence: An aside: From n = r² + 1 and r (the common degree) being an integer less than n–1, one may show that the only possible parameter sets for such a graph are those for which r ∈ {1, 2, 3, 7, 57} (the “Hoffman–Singleton” parameters and the “friendship theorem”‐related ones).
sentence-category-reason: Presents known parameter restrictions derived from earlier relations.

sentence: Since we require at least three persons can be seated around the table, the trivial r = 1 case (which would give n = 2) is excluded.
sentence-category-reason: Deductively excludes a parameter case based on the seating requirement.

sentence:
In the known cases,
  • r = 2 gives n = 5 (a 5–cycle itself),
  • r = 3 gives n = 10 (the Petersen graph),
  • r = 7 gives n = 50 (the Hoffman–Singleton graph),
  • r = 57 would give a graph on 3250 vertices (whose existence is a famous open problem).
sentence-category-reason: Lists known instances and their parameters; presents factual context.

sentence: In each case the girth is 5.
sentence-category-reason: States a property (girth 5) for the listed cases.
Section divider signaling conclusion.

sentence: The smallest number k of residents who can sit around a round table so that every pair of successive residents are friends (i.e. forming a cycle in the graph) is exactly 5.
sentence-category-reason: States the final value of k explicitly.

sentence: Thus the only possible value of k is 5.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the unique possible value for k.

sentence: Answer: k = 5.
sentence-category-reason: Explicit final answer statement.
